title: Child Survival Strategies II: Female Education, Family Planning, Post-Natal Exercises, Food Supplements, Water and Sanitation
introduction: Beyond clinic-based interventions, sustainable child survival depends on empowered mothers, planned birth spacing, maternal postpartum recovery, balanced weaning nutrition, safe drinking water, and hygienic sanitation. These intersecting Primary Health Care (PHC) strategies address the root social and environmental determinants of childhood morbidity and mortality.
learningOutcomes: 5.1 Define female education, evaluate its impact on child survival and national development, and identify strategies and barriers to promoting women's education.
5.2 Define family planning, evaluate the seven factors governing contraceptive choice, and classify barrier, hormonal, IUD, permanent, and unreliable contraceptive methods.
5.3 Explain the purpose, safe commencement timelines, and progressive routines of post-natal abdominal exercises following normal versus caesarean delivery.
5.4 Distinguish supplementary/weaning feeds from dietary supplements, state weaning food hygiene rules, and evaluate supplement safety risks.
5.5 Describe the physiological roles, purification methods, and daily requirements of water, and classify sanitation types and their health impacts.

content.heading: Female Education: Child Survival Impact, Promotion, Barriers, and National Development
content.body: Female education is the moral and intellectual training of females through formal schooling to acquire knowledge and skills—recognized as a fundamental human right under Article 26 of the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights (free compulsory elementary education, accessible technical/higher education on merit) and Chapter Four of the Nigerian Constitution prohibiting discrimination. Educating a woman educates an entire family because maternal educational status is a principal determinant of early child health: educated mothers achieve higher child survival rates, practise exclusive breastfeeding and improved nutrition, seek prenatal care (100% vs. 50% in uneducated mothers in cited comparisons) and childhood immunization far more consistently, desire smaller families, and utilize modern contraception effectively. Promoting female education requires eight coordinated actions: (1) orienting parents, communities, and religious leaders; (2) communicating education's tangible gains to parents; (3) enforcing laws against female child labour and street hawking; (4) discouraging teenage/early marriage and teenage pregnancy; (5) dismantling cultural/religious biases favouring boys' schooling; (6) eliminating gender bias in teaching and curricula; (7) employing more female teachers in rural areas as mentors/role models; and (8) reviewing curricula for gender sensitivity. Key hindrances include menstrual health challenges causing dropout, cultural early marriage, and sexual predation. Nationally, educated Nigerian women—exemplified by Prof. Grace Alele-Williams (first female VC, UNIBEN), Chief Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti (activist), Tejuoso (industrialist), and Prof. Dora Akunyili—build civic leadership across medicine, law, pharmacy, engineering, and politics.

content.heading: Family Planning and Classification of Contraceptive Methods
content.body: According to WHO, family planning (contraception/birth control) goes beyond preventing unwanted pregnancy to timing conception so every child is wanted; maintaining birth intervals of at least 2 years significantly improves maternal and infant survival. Selecting a method depends on seven factors: Health Status (coital frequency and childbearing desires), Effectiveness (failure rate), Affordability, Health Risk, Partner Involvement, Permanence (temporary vs. permanent), and Availability. Contraceptives fall into five main groups: (1) Barrier Methods—Condoms (latex male/female sheaths preventing sperm entry, requiring no prescription, and uniquely protecting against STDs), Diaphragm and Cervical Cap (provider-fitted rubber cup with spermicide over the cervix, left 6+ hours post-coitus; risks include irritation, UTI, rare toxic shock syndrome if left too long, or abnormal Pap with cap), and Vaginal Sponge (moistened spermicide-saturated synthetic sponge); (2) Hormonal Methods—using oestrogen plus progestin or progestin alone to inhibit ovulation and thicken cervical mucus: combined pills, progestin-only mini-pills, subdermal implants, 3-monthly progestin injections (Depo-Provera), skin patches (Ortho Evra), vaginal rings (NuvaRing), and emergency ('morning after') contraception; (3) Intrauterine Device (IUD)—provider-inserted plastic/copper or progestin-releasing uterine device lasting 5–10+ years with <1% annual failure (risks: cramps, heavy bleeding, uterine perforation; progestin IUD may cause spotting then amenorrhoea reversible on removal); (4) Permanent Methods—Tubal Ligation (severing/blocking fallopian tubes) and Vasectomy (blocking vas deferens); and (5) Unreliable / Natural Methods—Coitus Interruptus (withdrawal; pre-ejaculatory semen risks pregnancy), Post-coital Douching (ineffective as sperm pass the cervix within seconds), Fertility Awareness (charting basal temperature, cervical mucus, or calendar), Breastfeeding (lactation alone does not guarantee infertility), and Complete Abstinence (the only 100% effective method against pregnancy and STDs, though difficult to sustain).

content.heading: Post-Natal Exercises
content.body: Post-natal exercises are targeted muscular activities for the abdomen, uterus, thighs, perineum, lungs/diaphragm, back, and waist designed to aid uterine involution and restore abdominal muscle tone stretched during pregnancy. Mothers may begin gentle post-natal exercises roughly 3 weeks after a normal vaginal delivery and 7 weeks after a caesarean section. A structured progressive routine includes: (1) Weeks 3–5—lying supine with knees bent and feet flat, slowly lifting only the head off the floor while pulling the abdominals toward the spine on exhalation; complemented by contracting abdominals toward the spine for 2 seconds at least 20 times daily while seated; (2) Weeks 6–11 (following the 6-week medical check-up clearance)—progressing to 30 repetitions up to 3 sets daily alongside back curls and knee rolls; and (3) Post-Natal Sit-Ups (after 6 weeks)—lying with knees bent and feet flat, supporting the head in hands, slowly lifting head and shoulders for two counts (exhaling up, inhaling down) for 30 reps x 3 sets daily, gradually increasing reps weekly to firm abdominal tone.

content.heading: Food Supplements, Weaning Hygiene, and Water
content.body: Food supplements complement the diet, while supplementary feeds replace breast milk when a mother is severely ill or unconscious. As lactation ends, weaning gradually introduces a balanced diet containing protein, fat, carbohydrates, minerals, vitamins, roughage, and water. Hygienic weaning demands clean sanitized food-contact surfaces complying with food sanitation laws; for milk feeds, a clean cup and spoon washed with soap and clean water is strongly preferred over feeding bottles and teats. Dietary supplements (such as calcium and vitamins D/E for bones, folic acid to prevent birth defects, and omega-3 fatty acids for heart health) are not drugs and cannot cure disease; because active ingredients can interact with prescribed medications or accumulate across fortified foods, consumers should assess benefits, safety risks, dosage, and duration, and report serious adverse reactions immediately. Water (H2O)—an odourless, tasteless clear liquid comprising ~72% of the human body—is indispensable for survival, digestion, nutrient/oxygen transport, waste excretion, thermoregulation, muscle tone, skin elasticity, blood pH (~7.4) maintenance, relieving constipation and fluid retention, metabolizing fat, and diluting urinary carcinogens to lower bladder/colon cancer risk. Existing as solid, liquid, and gas, water acquires minerals or sewage/industrial pollutants depending on its source. Purification removes impurities via screening, sedimentation, filtration, chlorination, boiling, and aeration (removing odours/tastes), while water hardness (salts/metals) is removed by boiling, adding sodium carbonate and lime, or filtering through zeolites. Health officials recommend drinking at least 8 glasses of clean water daily.

content.heading: Sanitation Types and Health Impacts
content.body: WHO defines sanitation as the provision of facilities and services for the safe disposal of human urine and faeces—broadly encompassing hygienic prevention of human contact with hazardous wastes (human/animal faeces, solid refuse, domestic/industrial/agricultural wastewater) and garbage/sewage management. Key sanitation approaches include: (1) Improved Sanitation—household-level human faeces management tracked under MDG/WHO-UNICEF targets; (2) On-Site Sanitation—collecting and treating waste at the point of deposition (pit latrines, septic tanks); (3) Food Sanitation—hygienic measures ensuring food safety; (4) Environmental Sanitation—controlling environmental disease-transmission links (solid waste, water/wastewater, industrial waste, noise/pollution); (5) Ecological Sanitation—hygienically recycling nutrients and water from human/animal waste; and (6) Wastewater Collection—sewer systems conveying wastewater to treatment plants for safe reuse or discharge. Inadequate sanitation and unsafe water drive poverty-linked diseases causing up to 5 million preventable waterborne deaths annually—led by diarrhoeal diseases (1.6–2.5 million deaths/year and accounting for nearly 50% of underweight children), alongside schistosomiasis, trachoma, faecal-oral infections, and soil-transmitted hookworm.

inTextQuestions.question: Why is a clean cup and spoon preferred over a feeding bottle and teat when giving supplementary milk feeds during weaning?
inTextQuestions.answer: A cup and spoon washed with soap and clean water are easier to keep hygienically clean, reducing microbial contamination and diarrhoeal disease risk compared with feeding bottles and teats.

inTextQuestions.question: Which contraceptive method uniquely provides protection against sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) in addition to preventing pregnancy, and which method is 100% effective?
inTextQuestions.answer: Condoms (barrier method) protect against STDs alongside pregnancy prevention; Complete Abstinence is the only method 100% effective against both pregnancy and STDs.

inTextQuestions.question: When can a mother safely start post-natal abdominal exercises after a normal vaginal delivery versus a caesarean section?
inTextQuestions.answer: About 3 weeks after a normal vaginal delivery and 7 weeks after a caesarean operation.

inTextQuestions.question: How is water hardness removed during water treatment, and how does aeration purify water?
inTextQuestions.answer: Water hardness (caused by salts and metals) is removed by boiling, adding sodium carbonate and lime, or filtering through natural/artificial zeolites; aeration saturates water with air to remove odours and unpleasant tastes.

saqs.question: Define female education, explain how maternal education improves child survival, and list five ways to promote women's education in Nigeria.
saqs.answer: Female education is training females morally and intellectually through formal schooling. Educated mothers have higher child survival via exclusive breastfeeding, better nutrition, prenatal care, higher immunization uptake, and planned family sizes. Five promotion measures: orienting parents and religious/community leaders, prohibiting female child labour/street hawking, discouraging teenage marriage/pregnancy, removing cultural and curricular gender biases, and employing more female teachers in rural areas as mentors.

saqs.question: List the seven factors influencing contraceptive choice and explain how hormonal contraceptives and IUDs prevent pregnancy.
saqs.answer: Seven factors: health status, effectiveness, affordability, health risk, partner involvement, permanence, and availability. Hormonal methods (combined pills, mini-pills, implants, Depo-Provera injections, patches, vaginal rings, emergency pills) prevent ovulation and use progestin to thicken cervical mucus blocking sperm. IUDs (copper/plastic or progestin-releasing uterine devices) remain in place 5–10+ years with <1% annual pregnancy rate.

saqs.question: Describe the progressive post-natal abdominal exercise regimen from Weeks 3–5 through Weeks 6–11 and post-natal sit-ups.
saqs.answer: Weeks 3–5 (starting ~3 wks post-normal delivery / 7 wks post-C/S): lie supine with knees bent/feet flat, lift only the head while exhaling and drawing abdominals toward spine, plus 20 daily 2-second seated abdominal contractions. Weeks 6–11 (after 6-week doctor check-up): progress to 30 reps x 3 sets daily. Post-natal sit-ups: knees bent, hands supporting head, lift head and shoulders for 2 counts exhaling up/inhaling down for 30 reps x 3 sets daily.

saqs.question: State the five safety questions a person should ask before taking dietary supplements and list six methods of water purification.
saqs.answer: Five questions: (1) What are the product's potential benefits? (2) What are its benefits for me? (3) Does it have safety risks? (4) What is the proper dose? (5) How, when, and for how long should I take it? Six water purification methods: screening, sedimentation, filtration, chlorination, boiling, and aeration.

saqs.question: Define sanitation according to WHO, differentiate on-site sanitation from ecological sanitation, and summarize the major health impacts of poor sanitation.
saqs.answer: WHO defines sanitation as providing facilities and services for safe disposal of human urine and faeces. On-site sanitation collects and treats waste where deposited (pit latrines, septic tanks), whereas ecological sanitation hygienically recycles nutrients and water from human/animal waste. Poor sanitation drives up to 5 million annual waterborne deaths—including 1.6–2.5 million diarrhoeal deaths/year (causing ~50% of underweight children), schistosomiasis, trachoma, faecal-oral diseases, and hookworm.
